books.section: Great Depression and the New Deal (1929-1939)

primary_sources: Herbert Hoover, address accepting the Republican presidential nomination, August 11, 1928

stimulus.text: “We in America today are nearer to the final triumph over poverty than ever before in the history of any land. The poorhouse is vanishing from among us. We have not yet reached the goal, but, given a chance to go forward with the policies of the last 8 years, we shall soon with the help of God be in sight of the day when poverty will be banished from this Nation.” — Herbert Hoover, speech accepting the Republican presidential nomination, August 11, 1928. Abridged.
stimulus.source_note: Herbert Hoover, address accepting the Republican presidential nomination, Stanford, California, August 11, 1928. Verbatim excerpt, abridged; public domain.

source: original; stimulus verbatim from Herbert Hoover, address accepting the Republican presidential nomination, August 11, 1928, public domain
stem: Hoover's statement best reflects which of the following attitudes in 1928?

options.text: Fear that the stock market was about to collapse
options.misconception: Hoover shows no fear here. He says America is near the final triumph over poverty.

options.text: Confidence that Republican policies had nearly ended poverty
Support for direct federal relief to the unemployed
options.misconception: Hoover opposed direct federal relief. The passage promises prosperity through existing policies, not relief.

options.text: Opposition to the protective tariff on imported goods
options.misconception: Hoover says nothing about tariffs here, and he later signed the Hawley-Smoot Tariff of 1930.

rationales.A: Hoover says the poorhouse is vanishing and poverty will soon be banished, the opposite of fear about the market.
rationales.B: Hoover says that going forward with the policies of the last 8 years will soon bring the day when poverty is banished from the nation.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Hoover feared direct federal payments would foster dependence, and he refused them throughout his presidency.
rationales.D: Background from the books: Hoover signed the Hawley-Smoot Tariff in 1930, raising tariffs to near record levels.
rationales.general:
1. Read Hoover's claim: America is near the final triumph over poverty.
2. Ask what he credits: the policies of the last 8 years.
3. Ask what mood that is: confidence, not fear or doubt.
4. The statement reflects confidence that Republican policies had nearly ended poverty.
Remember: a campaign promise shows what a candidate believed, so read its mood first.
